lead: A voltage source inverter holds its DC voltage steady with a capacitor and lets the load decide the current. A current source inverter (CSI) does the opposite: a large series inductor L<sub>d</sub> holds the DC link current I<sub>d</sub> almost constant, and the bridge steers that current into the load lines. The output current is a rectangular wave of height I<sub>d</sub> and the load voltage is whatever the load needs. CSIs survive load short circuits well and regenerate easily, so they are used in megawatt motor drives and induction heating. Some syllabi call it the current-fed inverter.
prereq: You need: thyristor commutation (see Commutation techniques: natural and forced) and the three-phase bridge of 180° and 120° conduction.

sections.h3: Hold the current, not the voltage

blocks.text: A CSI is fed from a controlled rectifier or a chopper through L<sub>d</sub>. The inductor makes the link current stiff: over one output cycle I<sub>d</sub> hardly changes. The bridge can only choose which load lines carry it, so the switches must never open the current path. If every path opened, L<sub>d</sub> di/dt would destroy the devices, so the incoming device is turned on before the outgoing one is turned off (an overlap), the opposite of the dead time in a VSI.

Because the load voltage reverses every half cycle, an off device sees reverse voltage. A thyristor blocks it by itself; an IGBT needs a diode in series. Regeneration is easy: the front-end rectifier reverses V<sub>d</sub> while I<sub>d</sub> keeps its direction, so power flows back to the supply.

Four thyristors T1 to T4 form a bridge fed with I<sub>d</sub>, and a capacitor C is connected across the load. Firing T1 and T2 sends +I<sub>d</sub> into the load-and-capacitor pair; firing T3 and T4 sends −I<sub>d</sub>. The load current is a square wave of ±I<sub>d</sub> split between R and C.

Commutation is done by the capacitor. While T1, T2 conduct, C charges with the load side positive at the terminal T1 feeds. When T3 and T4 are fired, that capacitor voltage appears in reverse across T1 and T2, their current falls to zero at once (I<sub>d</sub> moves to T3, T4) and they stay reverse-biased while C discharges through the load and recharges the other way. With a resistive load the capacitor voltage at each switching is V<sub>0</sub> = I<sub>d</sub> R tanh(T/4RC), where T is the output period.

blocks.where: t<sub>c</sub> is the circuit turn-off time in seconds; it must exceed the thyristor turn-off time t<sub>q</sub>. When the half period is long compared with RC, t<sub>c</sub> = RC ln 2 = 0.693RC.

blocks.text: The three-phase form of this circuit, with commutating capacitors and series diodes that isolate them from the load, is the auto-sequential commutated inverter (ASCI).

Six devices conduct for 120° each, two at a time, one from the upper group and one from the lower. From 0° to 60° devices 6 and 1 conduct, so I<sub>d</sub> enters line A and returns through B; then 1 and 2 (A to C), 2 and 3 (B to C), 3 and 4 (B to A), 4 and 5 (C to A), 5 and 6 (C to B). Each line current is +I<sub>d</sub> for 120°, zero for 60°, −I<sub>d</sub> for 120°, zero for 60°: the same shape as the 180° VSI line voltage.
I1 = (√6/π)Id = 0.780Id, Irms = 0.816Id I1 is the rms fundamental line current and Irms the rms of the whole wave.

The 120° shape has no triplen harmonics (cos 3 × 30° = 0); the 5th is 20 % of the fundamental, the 7th 14.3 %, the 11th 9.1 % and the 13th 7.7 %, a THD of 31.1 %. With a motor, capacitors at its terminals take the harmonic currents, so the motor voltage comes out nearly sinusoidal.

A load-commutated inverter (LCI) uses the back EMF of an over-excited synchronous motor, which runs at a leading power factor, to turn its thyristors off, and drives motors of several megawatts in pumps, fans and compressors. At standstill there is no EMF, so the LCI starts by pulsing the link current to zero at each commutation until the motor has speed.

figure.caption: The second worked example: I<sub>d</sub> = 20 A is steered through T1, T2 or T3, T4 into 10 Ω with 20 μF across it. At each switching the capacitor voltage, ±197.3 V, reverse-biases the outgoing pair; it stays negative across them for t<sub>c</sub> = 137.3 μs, more than three times their 40 μs turn-off time.

spec.aria: Circuit of a single-phase current source inverter: a DC source and series inductor feed four thyristors, with a resistor and capacitor in parallel between the bridge midpoints. Below, the capacitor voltage over one 2 millisecond period rises exponentially to plus 197 volts, jumps sign at each switching, and the shaded turn-off intervals of 137 microseconds are marked.

examples.question: A three-phase CSI with 120° conduction has I<sub>d</sub> = 50 A and feeds a star-connected resistive load of 2 Ω per phase. Find (a) the rms fundamental line current, (b) the total rms line current, (c) the fundamental and total load power, and (d) the rms harmonic current and the THD.
steps: (c) Star load, so the line current is the phase current. P<sub>1</sub> = 3 I<sub>1</sub>² R = 3 × 38.98² × 2 = 9119 W; P = 3 I<sub>rms</sub>² R = 3 × 40.82² × 2 = 10000 W.
examples.answer: I<sub>1</sub> = 38.98 A, I<sub>rms</sub> = 40.82 A, P<sub>1</sub> = 9.12 kW of P = 10.00 kW, I<sub>h</sub> = 12.12 A and THD = 31.1 %.

examples.question: A single-phase capacitor-commutated CSI has I<sub>d</sub> = 20 A, load R = 10 Ω, commutating capacitor C = 20 μF and output frequency 500 Hz. The thyristors have t<sub>q</sub> = 40 μs. Find the peak load voltage, the circuit turn-off time and the safety margin.
steps: Peak load voltage V<sub>0</sub> = I<sub>d</sub> R tanh(T/4RC) = 20 × 10 × tanh 2.50 = 200 × 0.9866 = 197.3 V.
t<sub>c</sub> = RC ln(1 + tanh(T/4RC)) = 200 × ln 1.9866 = 200 × 0.6864 = 137.3 μs (the long-period value RC ln 2 is 138.6 μs).
Margin: t<sub>c</sub>/t<sub>q</sub> = 137.3/40 = 3.4, so the thyristors have ample time to recover.
examples.answer: V<sub>0</sub> = 197.3 V peak, t<sub>c</sub> = 137.3 μs, about 3.4 times the 40 μs turn-off time.

traps: I<sub>d</sub> is the height of the current wave, not its rms: the fundamental rms is 0.78I<sub>d</sub> and the total rms 0.816I<sub>d</sub>.
A CSI needs overlap between incoming and outgoing devices, not dead time; an open circuit, not a short circuit, is the dangerous fault.
The diode with each CSI switch is in series, for reverse blocking; the VSI diode is anti-parallel, for feedback.
In the capacitor-commutated CSI, the turn-off time is RC ln 2 only when the half period is long compared with RC.
A grid-tied inverter controls its current but has a capacitor DC link, so it is a VSI, not a CSI.

quiz.q: What makes the DC link of a CSI stiff, and what does it hold constant?
quiz.a: A large series inductor L<sub>d</sub>; it holds the link current I<sub>d</sub> nearly constant.

quiz.q: Why does each IGBT in a CSI need a series diode?
quiz.a: The load voltage reverses each half cycle, so an off device is reverse-biased. An IGBT blocks almost no reverse voltage; the series diode does. A thyristor blocks it by itself.

quiz.q: A three-phase CSI with 120° conduction has I<sub>d</sub> = 80 A. Find the rms fundamental and total rms line current.
A single-phase capacitor-commutated CSI feeds R = 5 Ω at low frequency. Find the smallest C for t<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 30 μs.
quiz.a: At low frequency t<sub>c</sub> = 0.693RC, so C = 60 μs/(0.693 × 5) = 17.3 μF.

quiz.q: An LCI drive cannot start a synchronous motor by load commutation alone. Why, and what is done?
quiz.a: Load commutation needs the motor EMF to reverse-bias the outgoing thyristor; at standstill there is none. The rectifier pulses I<sub>d</sub> to zero at each commutation (pulsed mode) until the motor reaches about a tenth of its speed.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a CSI tolerates a load short circuit better than a VSI.
quiz.a: The link inductor limits the rate of rise of current, and the current controller keeps I<sub>d</sub> at its set value; a VSI's capacitor would discharge straight into the fault.

beyond: Not for the exam. Medium-voltage drives use PWM current-source inverters with gate-commutated thyristors and output capacitors for a near-sine motor current. Reverse-blocking IGBTs remove the series diode. Search for PWM current source inverter and load-commutated inverter starting.
